sentences.text: The genus name Eucoelophysis translates to "true hollow form" in Ancient Greek, while the specific species name honors the collector David Baldwin.
This animal is classified within the family Silesauridae.
Because of unclear vertebral features and pelvic differences, scientists currently accept only the hindlimb as definitive material for the species.
In 1887, Edward Drinker Cope initially classified specimens collected by David Baldwin as Coelurus bauri and Coelurus longicollis.
Two years later, in 1889, Cope created the new genus Coelophysis for three species from New Mexico.
In 1996, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature designated a skeleton from Whitaker Quarry as the holotype of Coelophysis bauri.
In 2000, Andrew Heckert and colleagues identified fossils from the Snyder Quarry that may belong to Eucoelophysis.
An articulated skeleton was moved to Eucoelophysis in 2009 but returned to Coelophysis in 2018 due to taxonomic re-evaluation.
Research indicates that Eucoelophysis is a close relative of Silesaurus and forms the sister group to Dinosauria.
Studies confirm that it is not a theropod or dinosaur but is related to Silesaurus and Pseudolagosuchus.
It is debated whether Eucoelophysis represents a primitive ornithischian, though it is confirmed as a dinosauriform.
Eucoelophysis lived during the Late Triassic, specifically the Norian period, in the Chinle Formation of New Mexico.
Its time range is estimated to span from 227.3 to 201.4 million years ago.
The bonebed locality where these fossils were found also included other reptiles such as Typothorax.
